overview: The Safavids, who took Tabriz in 1501, made Twelver Shia Islam the religion of Iran and gave the country the shape and identity it has kept since. Shah Abbas I's Isfahan, the carpets, the painted manuscripts and the long wars with the Ottomans mark their two centuries.

items.text: Shah Abbas I made Isfahan his capital and laid out the Naqsh-e Jahan square with the Shah Mosque, the Sheikh Lotfollah mosque and the Ali Qapu palace.
The Ardabil carpet of 1539 to 1540 and the court workshops set the standard for Persian carpets, which reached European palaces by the thousands.
Reza Abbasi and the Isfahan painters, and the Shahnameh made for Shah Tahmasp with its 258 miniatures.
Ismail I proclaimed Twelver Shia Islam the state religion at Tabriz and brought Shia scholars from Lebanon and Iraq to teach it.
A clerical hierarchy, the shrines of Mashhad and Qom and the mourning rites of Muharram took root.
Armenian Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians lived as protected communities, with periods of pressure.
Shah Abbas moved Armenian merchants from Julfa to New Julfa in Isfahan; their network carried Iranian silk to Venice, Amsterdam and India.
Isfahan grew into one of the largest cities of the seventeenth century, with its bazaar, bridges and gardens.
Twelver Shia Islam remains Iran's state religion.
Naqsh-e Jahan square was listed by UNESCO.
Carpets and miniature painting remain the arts Iran is known for.

fall.text: Afghan rebels took Isfahan in 1722 after a siege. Nader, an Afshar Turkmen general, drove them out, ruled through puppet Safavid shahs, and took the crown himself as Nader Shah in 1736.
